sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Arnold R. Green. Mr. Green was a construction worker working for the Navy on Wake Island when the war began. He was later officially designated a Seabee. Arnold was a prisoner of war on Wake Island and in Japan. I am Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Green's home in Strongsville, Ohio on April 20th, 2004. Arnold was 80 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So let's see, I'm not sure where to start here. Let's start with when did you get to Wake Island.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, I went to Wake Island. I got a job with Morrison Knudson when I was 18 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of company was that?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Morrison Knudson, it was probably the largest construction company in the world. As a matter of fact, there is an office right down here in downtown Cleveland still operating. And I took a job on Wake Island. I went there to work as a, as a matter of fact I have got the -- On the dredge. And of course, I was glad to get the job because it was paying 140 dollars a month and this was 1941, and not too many people made that kind of money. So, we were out there building a destroyer base and an airstrip. What I am looking for is something that just showed up recently from the Japanese government. Oh, for goodness sake. Where did I put it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Eighteen years old. I was the youngest person on that island. One other guy, Bill May, he says he thought he was the youngest one and we figured out I was the youngest one. But that is no claim to fame really. Well, someplace in here I have got it. And as a matter of fact, I had Professor Banks interpret it. It's all in Japanese. And it deals with, we were -- What made it very interesting is that I was, we were in a camp called Camp -- We were in Camp 18. There is no record in the archives of Camp 18.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Not now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not in the Japanese archives anywhere?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, not in ours.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not in ours? Oh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: They list all the Prisoner of War camps except Camp 18. But this, and I wanted to show you this, as a matter of fact here is a translation of it right here. That is the translation that I got of it. And they, the Japanese admittedly there was a Camp 18. And it was at Fukuoka, and it was the camp where all the guys, my friends and that, most of them died right there. As a matter of fact, I was part of a group of 350 and 187 died in that prison camp. They didn't make --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I would like to -- Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, go ahead.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I was going to say let's get back to were you fresh out of high school when you took this job?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, I had got a job, I had joined the Three Cs. I was out in Oregon. Morrison and Knudson is headquartered in Boise, Idaho and they sent a letter out to Three C camps that they were looking for labor and the offer was very good so I took them up on that. That is -- Went to Wake. As a matter of fact there was six of us started out. One of the fellows still lives in Louisville Kentucky, Sis James. But he went to Midway. Three went to Midway and three went to Wake.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you arrived on Wake in 1941?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I arrived in Wake in 1941 on, let's see, September, well six weeks before the war started. I actually have still my original contract that I signed at that time to go to Wake Island.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the company?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, my job with them was what they called a, it was a Dredge Shore Laborer. And at that time I got a job on what they called the "bull gang." We were the ones that put the dead men in for the -- because the dredge itself could not function without the -- They had no -- the swing made move so they used dead men along the shore. That was part of the job and that is where I worked. And we, as a matter of fact, I am still going to still look for this because I want you to see it and I'll keep talking at the same time. We, on December 8th when, it was December the 8th or 7th, when they attacked Pearl Harbor, they attacked Pearl Harbor at 7:00 o'clock in the morning.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: They attacked us at 11:00 o'clock. We were told that the war had started and that we had to get the island ready for an invasion. So, my best friend and I, we were, Paul Gosslin, we were assigned the job of tying up the floating lines. This was on what they called Peale island. There is three islands out there. As a matter of fact, give you a little idea of Wake, Wake is, there is ten square miles -- or two and a half square miles of land and it's ten miles from tip-to-tip, fifteen feet above sea level. You can stand on one side of the island and see the ocean breaking on the other side. It's that small. Anyway so Paul and I were there when they came over and I guess this is what you want to know is what actually happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: So we were expecting a flight of B-17s because that is what he were told were coming from Midway. And we saw this, at 11:00 o'clock in the morning there is like a line in the sky. They weren't B-17s, they were Mitsubishi jet bombers. There were 32 of them. And they came in and at 1500 feet which made it impossible for us, for them to cut the fuses on the three inch shells short enough that they would be effective. And we didn't give the Japanese credit for what they could do. They hit everything they wanted on that island. We had 12 airplanes. Actually, there is, the picture you are looking at is what some of them looked like when it was over with. They had 12. They destroyed eight of them the first day. The four they didn't destroy were flying or it's possible they would have got all of them the first day. They hit every warehouse on the island. Got all of our oil storage. And it came in and I had no idea what it was, all of is sudden you are in water. Paul and I were out in Peale, Peale Island at the sea plane ramp and tying up the floating line. And they had told us don't get in the lagoon during an air raid because if they drop a bomb in the lagoon, the concussion could kill you. Well, Paul jumped in the lagoon. I jumped under a pipe. And as a matter of fact, just recently, I, Professor Banks and I get together and there was a Marine there that had been stationed on Wake and I asked him, he said oh, the bullet holes are still in that sea plane right where I had been standing, this guy was shooting. But you could see them actually, they weren't that far. So that started the war for us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What happened to Paul then?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, Paul got killed the second day. We had gone back to the, we had gone back to the barracks to get a few personal things and the air raid, they came over again and Paul ran around me. I went to one end of the barracks and jumped in the sewer line and Paul ran to the other and they dropped the bomb just as he was coming out the door. Never knew what hit him, I guess. And I can relate to pretty much everything that happened those fifteen days, but I can't relate to the day after that. It's completely like a blank in my mind. And I miss Paul. Paul and I were very, very close. And at that time, of course, then I got tied up with the guys that were -- Well, we were all working together to defend the island, but I got tied up with the, there were six Army people on the island, 350 Marines and 100 from the Marine Air Corps and I got tied up with the six Army people because they had been sent to the island to set up a radio station there to bring in the B-17s and I could use a key. I had been trained to use a key, so I got the wireless people. As a matter of fact, I contend that my message did get through to Pearl Harbor. I'm not sure, but the one I sent got in I understand. But that is who I got hooked up with. And that was the start of the thing for me at that time. Everybody else was involved. We were either filling sandbags or moving guns or carrying ammunition. So everybody got involved into it. They moved those guns every night. And that was a chore. And I guarantee you, nobody can carry a box of three inch shells by himself, no way, nobody, unless you are super ____________. We lasted fifteen days. As a matter of fact on the 11th of December, the Japanese showed up to invade the island. And we sank two destroyers and drove them off. Now, and the final thing at Wake Island is probably one of the most embarrassing victories the Japanese ever had because their casualty count was between five and 7000. We lost 125 people and we always kind of felt that is why they did what they did to us. In that day there they lost two destroyers. They came back on the 23rd, but they were ready now. They came back with two aircraft carriers, some heavy cruisers and a bunch of the -- the Japanese had a special invading group, you know, they were the Imperial Marines. And even for what it's worth, we didn't, we underestimated, I said we underestimated, we underestimated what they even looked like. These guys were six foot at all and when they came up that beach they looked like they just came off of a dress parade. They were pretty tough. Anyway, when they came the 23rd and, of course, we surrendered. I'm not proud that we surrendered, none of us were, but we did surrender.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How were you able to sink the destroyers? Was that artillery or air attacks?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, what we had on Wake Island, for what it was worth we had three batteries of five inch rifles. You're not supposed to sink -- and we sank a light cruiser with that and you're not supposed to do that with five inch rifles and the Marines did it. And we had three batteries of three inch anti-aircraft and I don't remember how many .50 calibers we hit, but that was our defense. And the final thing at the tail end there, the Japanese there, we got bombed every day. You could almost sit there and watch, because like at 11:00 o'clock in the morning they'd come over and they'd hit us again. And they had pretty much destroyed our range finders and this and that. So, as a matter of fact, that is why at the tail end, the one plane we had left, what he would do, he would get up and fly and get up on the same level with the Japanese bombers and radio back down to tell the people on the three inch guns at what level the Japanese bomber was, because there was no way in the world to figure that out any other way. We did that. We only lasted fifteen days, but like I said, they paid dearly for that place.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So once they actually landed on the island, there wasn't much resistance that you could put up?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: We could have -- They were in a pocket on the island. They were in, right there at Peacock Point, I was above that up where the bunkers were, that is where I was. But they were there and they could have probably wiped them out. They really took a shellacking on that. Even like on the island of Wilkes, where they landed four __________, only two of them left. We had these, the Marines on Wake Island I believe were the original China Marines. And they were so dam mean it was unbelievable. They'd fight with each other if they didn't have somebody to fight with. But they were good. They were very good. When they took us prisoners, of course, the first thing they did to us we had to take off of all of our clothes. Stark raving naked out there. And Wake Island was like subtropical. I mean we got sunburned in places you never thought you'd get sunburned. They wired our hands behind our back and put it up, tied them up around our neck. So you actually, if you dropped your hands down, you would cut off, you'd strangle yourself. And made us sit down on that thing for the best part of two days, the 23rd and the 24th of December. 25th, they let us go back to our barracks. You know, and of course, one thing about the Japanese, the Japanese were cruel, very cruel. And I mean there is testimony to that, what they did at Bataan, what they did at Nanking (ph) and what they did, they were very cruel. And that is my complaint. The people a lot of times say to me, well, how do you feel about the Japanese. Japanese people are okay. It's their government that is accountable for what happened. You know, these guys wouldn't have done what they did if the Japanese government hadn't approved it. And they did do a lot of things. They all carried a stick. Lot of them were shaped like a Samurai sword and of course we all got our lumps. One thing we learned real fast is you always protected your face and your head because they didn't care where they hit you. And while we were on Wake, it wasn't bad, it wasn't living bad. As a matter of fact, what they had done, they had split us into two groups. They left 350 on Wake Island. That is where these guys got killed. They murdered them. They sent eleven hundred and some to Shanghai. As a matter of fact, we know for a fact that the guys they sent to Shanghai, before they got to Shanghai they took five of them out of the hold of that ship. The ship was the Nita Maru, an original Japanese luxury liner. Called them up on deck and charged them with the crime of killing Japanese and therefore they had to die. So they used them for live bayonet practice before they got there. On Wake Island there, the first thing that happened to me, they put me into a, like a group that was supposed to be deck hands and we helped unload the Japanese ships. Because Wake Island there is no way. They had to unload on the barges. That was our job. And in February of 1942, I got an attack of appendicitis. And our doctor at that time was a Doctor Shank from Indianola, Indiana, tremendous individual, tremendous. And he taught us things. He was just a great guy. I crawled out and I had a good attack, because I already thrown up the phlegm and everything else that goes with it. And I crawled out on the porch and the Japanese guard said you got to get back in. Nobody was allowed outside. Next morning I saw Doctor Shank and I said, he checked me out and he said, Arnold, you got appendicitis. What do you want to do about it? I didn't care because I was sick. And if I died right there, it wouldn't have made no difference. But anyway he said, so he went to the Japanese doctor to get something to knock me out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Anesthetic?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Anesthetic. They refused to give it to him. So, he came back that night to what was our hospital and him and Milt Dryer put me on a field stretcher and laced me like a mummy. So he operated on me without any anesthetic. And you know, there is no sensation, feeling of being cut. It's like you're being burned. I can still remember that. And part way through the operation Doctor Shank said geez, I didn't know arnold was so fat. And oh, I missed it. I have got to make another cut. So I have got a scar that big. But he took the appendix out and I survived. I'm here today. And so that was the first bit. But like when we were on Wake Island, like I said, we didn't live too bad. We were back in our own barracks. We were using our beds. As a matter of fact we were using their laundry on the island when they let us do that. And we were fed pretty good. Some of the stuff we had I'm not too sure of. We didn't know whether it was a cat or a dog or whatever they were feeding us, but we ate it. And in the meantime they were using us to get together. We had -- during the war while the fighting was going on we took the supplies and scattered them all over the island. And we'd go over and get something to eat. As a matter of fact, just getting back to that, when we were still in the course of defending the island, they had a guy by the name of Sergeant Wright. Biggest guy you ever saw. And he was in charge of our guys that were moving those three inch guns every night. And he wouldn't feed you till the guns were moved and sandbagged and that could be at 2:00, 3:00, 4:00 o'clock in the morning. Then they always said that the Japanese really were looking for him, because they killed him, they dropped a bomb close to his place and killed him and then blew him out of his grave the next day. But anyway, like I said, we weren't living too bad. We could have survived, but I'm glad because these were the guys we left on Wake Island. And in September, they divided us and they sent 250 of us to Japan. And Fukuoka, 90-some of them died that first year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You say they left, as far as leaving Wake Island, 98 of these guys anyway were murdered?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they just execute them or --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Just executed them. Took them down to beach, lined them up and killed them. I just want to show you a few things here. There is not many of us left, there is only five of us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Five of the civilians left or five of any --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Five of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- the people that were captured on Wake Island?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, at Camp 18 there is only five of us. The rest are dead.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were taken along with 250 guys to this camp?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah we went to Sasebo, that is Camp Fukuoka. And I am going to show you, this is Wake Island. That is the list of guys that if you go out there that monument would be there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you have been back to Wake Island since?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I'd love to go back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What is that?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I'd love to go back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: These are what we're looking at pictures here of the Memorial on Wake Island.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah, that and this is the rock that is out there that tells them where they murdered those 98.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It says 98 US POW 5/10/43, so that would be, what, October 5th?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: When they killed them. That is when they killed them. Some Jap did that. And we, as a matter of fact I have here a translation from a Jap soldier that kept a diary telling about what actually happened. The marine that I talked to is here, Professor Banks, he saw the rock. Let's see what I got here, give you a little idea. This is the picture of the dam that we built for them. They put a monument up there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where is this dam in Japan?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: In Japan, right near Fukuoka. Actually it's in the Soho district. That is where we lost all of our guys.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that trip from Wake to Japan like?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Oh, we were took over in a coal burning oil tanker. There was 250 of us traveling in what was the dining room and there wasn't any, we didn't have any luxury suites or anything. And we got to Japan and a couple times, well, one time we thought something had happened, because what it was they ran aground a little bit. But they got us to Japan. They took, we ended up at Yokohama. They marched us through town and the people all cheered and that. They were, Japan was actually winning the war at that time. That was in September and they were winning, and oh, they were glad to see us, and they loaded us on a train and took us down to, now we're on Yokohama. Yokohama is on the island of Hokkaido. They sent us down to Kyushu, which was the southern island. So they took us down there. And when we got to Sasebo we got, that was night and they marched us through town. And the Japanese shined their flashlights in our face and threw shit at us and threw garbage at us and poked us and the Jap guard thought it was good. And you know, the surprising thing is and I never thought about it until not too long ago, the abuse we got was while we were still held prisoners by the Japanese Navy. Japanese Army were bad, but nothing like the Navy. We got to this camp where we built this dam, we did everything. And you do a lot of this by hand. In other words, when they call ganzamayana (phonetic) a wicker basket to load the dirt in this coal cart in. But we worked in a rock crusher. That wasn't a bad deal either. That was a lot better than some of the other things. And if you got the sand pile that was even better, especially when, on warm days. But couple things happened there that, best I can give you and idea, we they, put they mixed us with a bunch of Koreans, Korean labor they brought in. And one time the Koreans said hey, you are going to get a "bow IQ." Well, hell, we knew what IQs are but we didn't know what the "bow" thing was. We found out found real quick. The bow is a stick. So every Jap sailor had a bamboo club only about two inches in diameter. And they broke us up into squads and they started beating us. And they beat us and they beat us and they beat us. And of course, not being smart or anything like that, I got up in front where they really got to working me over. I should have got on the tail end of the line because by that time you would be pretty tired. They did that to us three times. I climbed a guy -- and of course, where they put us in there was nothing like Wake. We were put into a cement shed. No heat at all. Nothing in there. We slept on the floor on straw mats with fleas and lice and everything else that goes with it. Like I said, no heat there at all. And one time, you weren't allowed to even get warm, I was caught one time standing by the Jap -- by the Korean's fire and the Japanese warrant officer come in called me up and he had me stand at attention. And he took a rock and started beating on me on the forehead to tell me that you are not supposed -- I knew what the hell he was beating me for. But by the time he was done I had a lump like that on my forehead. And then this, at one point there, why, I ran into a Japanese officer, Igawa Heso. I met him, he was up at the garage. I was on mess detail and I was going back to work. And he told me that he was afraid to go to Southern California, and he had been in the United States. And as a matter of fact, there was like a half dozen of them had originally been in the United States. One was a traffic cop in San Francisco. One had been a hobo that ran back and forth and one was a junk dealer in Chicago. So they were all, they had all been in the United States. But this guy said, and he was a ranking officer now. And he was going to take good care of us because he didn't believe all of that propaganda that was coming out of the Japanese newspapers, because we weren't really as bad as they said we were. Well, one of the first things he did, he started, not the first day, like I said I was there maybe there a month or so, it was what I call a trial, where they come into the barracks while we were sleeping at 2:00 o'clock in the morning and get everybody up. And then they would call out three names and charge them with trading -- The worse thing you could do was trade with the Koreans and we all did when we could. Then they'd come and charge you with that. What the hell would they call it? There is a name for the trial, it was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Like a mock trial or whatever.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Whatever it is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: And then they'd start beating on you and they would beat and just beat the hell out of you. Well, the second time they came in, they called, the first guy they called was the Frenchman. We had a lot of older people with us. One guy in there, the old blacksmith had to be in his 70s, but they called the Frenchman. And he had been in World War I and had been a prisoner of the Germans. They called him up and charged him with the same thing. And they started on him. And he passed out a couple times. They'd throw water on him and bring him back again and beat on him. Shit was running down his legs and that. And the next number they called was san baka rokujuuku (ph). That is Arnold Green. I was the next guy in line. And I don't mind telling you I was, that was the only time I can really remember being scared. And the old Jap, one of them, there was an old Jap sailor there came over and poked me on the chest. He said now they got you, Nopo, (ph) now they got you. So I don't know whether I was crying or what, but he said matai, matai (ph) stay here, and went up to the ASO and whatever he said, I don't know, but he come back and said get back in the muofus, get back in the blankets, get out of here. He saved my life that night. And then two days later the Frenchman died. How that guy could have withstood that beating, they just abused him. You know, and it was kind of funny, too, we had one visit by the Red Cross there. They came in and looked us over, but nothing ever really came out of it. I have got up here, if you want to see this, I don't have a whole lot of souvenirs, I didn't give a damn about souvenirs. I just wanted to get home. But there was a few things I did save. As a matter of fact I am going to speak out against it. I have got seven classes out here. This is, if you are interested in it, this is a list of all the guys that were on Wake Island.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ah.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: You might have a relative there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Possibly. But this is a list of, what, 350 guys?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, that is 1100.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 1100, okay.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Because they were, we were on -- This is a copy of my original contract with Morrison Knudson. If you want to see it, you are welcome to take a look at it. And then I don't know, I just --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. It says September 15th, 1941.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That is when I went to work for them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: They took us to the bank and arranged that we would get fifty dollars and we signed a note that -- Hell, I never saw fifty dollars at one time in my life at that time. But that was the contract I signed. And it was, we had a great -- My friend and I had made up our minds that when we finished our contract on Wake, we were going to stay with the company, because they had jobs all over the world. And we were just going to go all over the world. Follow them and we had it all figured out. But anyway, this here, is a letter I wrote my mother. That was on, I guess the 21st of December in '41. I was lucky enough to get a message off to my mother. I told her I was all right and I'd be coming home and just to be looking for me. They put it in the Cincinnati -- I was living in Cincinnati, but a lot of those guys didn't get letters off, but I --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you got letter a off, what did you say, September '43 or '41?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, no, no, December. Two days before we surrendered. When they sent the PBY in with some officers to see what we needed on Wake to survive, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The letter is not in here.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: It's not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The return, a little return note from 1944 was in there.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, but, they, I got it someplace. But my mother saved all of my letters. I saved all of this from her.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that mail that came while you were in the prison camp?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, some of it did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were able to get some letters out?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Some.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Some.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Took -- My mother didn't know I was alive for two years because if you checked, if you saw '44 on that, that is about '44 we started writing. And I don't know when this one is. This is a classic right here. But, where were we on this thing anyway?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So anyway, I guess, first of all for two years, your family, were you just listed as missing in action?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I don't know how they had us listed, but she didn't know but if you look at the dates on this --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This one is dated, actually the postmark is August 24th, 1944.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: So it was '43, '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This looks like, this is a post card that you sent back and it is dated just July of 1944.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That is it. So that is when we started corresponding. This is another one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I am going read this since we can't see it on the microphone. Dear mother, I am in good health. Hoping you are all the same. I hope to see you soon. Give my love to the family. Keep Joseph in school and not quit school like I did. Your son, Arnold.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: But you see, we were allowed twenty-five words. If you count there is twenty-five words there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 -- Well, you cheated a little bit. It's a little bit more than twenty-five.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: But that was all we could tell them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow, so you did actually, after two years --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah, some, and of course they had, there was a whole bunch of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. And these little post card things say Imperial Japanese Army on them. Here is one. Dear Mother, Doing swell, in good health. Wishing you and the rest of the family same. Pray for you all and a speedy reunion. Miss you all. Regards to relatives. Your loving son. And this one, I can't tell if it is postmarked so, yeah it was two years before they were able to find anything out. Wow. So what else can you tell me about life in that camp?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: The food, there wasn't that much food. Like I said, we slept in there. There was no heat. Are you finished with that --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I don't know if I have time to go through it right now.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: If you want to, you are welcome to it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, maybe after we --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: But, of course, we were all losing weight. I weighed a hundred -- I weighed fifty kilos when I got out of the prison camp. That is right at about 100, 110 pounds. I am 6'4". And I had made up my mind at that point and so did my friends, we weren't going to survive a winter in Japan. We couldn't. There was no way in the world we could have. But particularly this camp where we built this dam was probably the worse of them all. From what I started to tell you, we knew that our government was sending Red Cross packages. Never saw them. They found them after the war. There was warehouses full of them. And we know that the government gave two hundred million dollars that was supposed to provide medical supplies for us. Never showed up. Never showed up. But apparently the Japanese kept it. But getting back to this camp, how we were treated, you were getting banged around every day so you just got used to it. And we didn't realize how bad we were being treated. That is another thing. We never realized that. And the most important thing, most important thing was a spoon. If you got a chance to eat, you wanted to be ready for it. This was one that the Black Dutch made for me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was made by somebody in the camp?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very nice work. Did this food come back from the camp too?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: This is my spoon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: You see it's worked on, they got "Lofty" on there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That is what it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A R Green, Cincinnati O, USA, Lofty.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That is me. My tag.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What is that?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Told you who I was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is your, a wooden dog tag, basically. Did you, when you were in that camp building this dam, did that take most of the time you were there? How long did it take to construct that dam?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, we didn't finish it completely. Actually, we were pretty well on our way to finishing it when they transferred us to another camp. But that is where most of our people died. As a matter of fact, I have got a list of all of them. I have kept it and I'll never forget it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did most of the people die there from malnutrition?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Strictly malnutrition. Strictly malnutrition. Because, and there was no medical thing, doctors or anything like that. This is an interesting thing that maybe would be interesting, but we're jumping ahead of this, because we were in four camps. This is the order that was picked up by General MacArthur when they was in Taiwan. This is the order that had been sent out to all the Commanders of all the Japanese prison camps what to do. They didn't care how they did it, just kill them all if there was an invasion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let me see this here. Wow. Okay. This is overwhelming. Let me see if I can kind of get this on tape, the gist of it. This is an order that was sent to the camp commanders I assume, for the various prison camps --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- in Japan or well, probably anywhere.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That was prior to --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Prior to the invasion of Japan?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Am I reading this date right? It says August 1st, 1944.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They are talking about if there are explosions, etcetera, in moving the prisoners and that sort of thing and under heavy guard the preparation for the final disposition will be made. And they are referring, of course, to the disposition of the prisoners, right? The time and method of this disposition are as follows: The time, although the basic aim is to act under superior orders, individual disposition may be made in the following circumstances: When an uprising of large numbers cannot be suppressed without the use of firearms, when escapees from the camp may turn into a hostile fighting force. The methods, whether they are destroyed individually or in groups or however it is done, with mass bombing, poisonous smoke, poisons, drowning, decapitation or what, dispose of them as the situation dictates. And also under that category: In any case, it is the aim not to allow the escape of a single one, to annihilate them all and not to leave any traces. And it's to the commanding general, to the commanding general, military police.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Whew!

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: So, I was lucky to come home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This particular document was apparently not declassified until July of 1974.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So for thirty years, nobody knew.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Nobody knew. See that is what McArthur's people picked up and translated in Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did MacArthur know that this was the plan?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I don't know. I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Right there they say what it was. But anyway to go back to that there short trial, what progressed from there is we, they transferred us to a new camp. Trying to think if there was something we may have missed. Anyway, the new camp was now instead of building a dam we were building an airstrip. And the camp was supposed to have been a summer camp. It was a framework of two-by-twos and covered with bark. This is when they brought in the -- Oh, one thing I failed to tell you was that, this is my notebook. I started to keep a diary.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That is made out of a cement sack. We put the cement sacks to good use there. What we would do is we would tear the cement sacks and wrap them around our legs and arms and our body to keep warm and tied them on. It served that purpose. This way, you see a notebook out of it. Lot of names in there and lot of people from all over the world.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. Pretty amazing.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Anyway, at this new camp -- Oh, this is, now this is a list of -- and I knew most of these guys that died in that, died from our group of our 350.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any particularly close buddies from this group?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Very well. Sure, I do. I think about them, sometimes I even cry. Doctor Shank, Milt Dryer, Gottlieb -- Whatchamacallit -- but I sure remember them. Irwin Miller, they were all friends of mine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It looks like this list is, what, 111 names?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I don't know. You have got them on both sides.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, that looks like, so it's 111 out of the 350 that were sent from Wake.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: And then the 98 on Wake.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And then the 98, of course, on Wake that were murdered.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: So it was, yeah, so it was over 50 percent of them guys didn't make it. In this new camp we were in down there, they found some flour some place. They gave it to us. See we made "sting bread" out of it. It was just like glue though. And the camp where I was, we had rats. What you are holding in your hand is my prayer book. And if you look at the back of it, see that cover had come off, so I took some of the bread and glued it back on. Well, at night the rats ate the glue off of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They ate the bread glue.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the prayer book that you had with you the whole time?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Oh, yeah, that was my prayer book. And that was at the various camps and I keep this and show it to the kids. We, like I said, we were building this airstrip and things didn't get any better. As a matter of fact, they were same crap. This is a list of a lot of the guys that were with me. The little bit of the diary that I kept on the island there. But anyway after we worked on that thing for a while and we were all losing weight and that and we were all getting skinny. And you know, there is no medical help. I mean, if you got sick, hey, that is too bad, you just take care of yourself. And then they moved us then into probably what was the, we couldn't, it was probably the best camp we went into. It was a brand new one and it was dug into the ground about four feet, so it functioned just like a air raid shelter as well as a place to sleep. But it was always the same thing. You slept on the floor. You had the fleas and the lice. As a matter of fact, we had one guy in our outfit that had brought a marine blanket from Wake Island and he made himself and he sowed himself into it. When he died we cut it off. He was completely covered with lice, the lice had killed him. * * * END OF DISK ONE. BEGIN DISK TWO. * * * BY MR. GREEN:

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: (Interruption of audio) -- they had about six inches of scum on top. You'd push it aside and you'd get in and clean them, but we had to. Some of us were mixing cement and that is what we did. We looked like statutes when we come out of that. And no soap. We didn't have any soap. They never gave it. So you really would scrub. So what we did, we improvised. And we had to be, we must have smelled like something else. We had to. We'd get coral sponges. And I don't know if you know what a coral sponge is, but this is not a soft sponge at all and it was like a piece of sandpaper. And that is what you would do to get your dirt and filth off of you. No medical care, nothing at all. So that was it, I can remember that. This other camp I just told you about where it was supposed to be a summer camp, same story all over again. But here they had mixed us in with a bunch of English and White and Black Dutch. I don't know if you know what Black Dutch are.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Black Dutch are from Indonesia. They were that, so the White Dutch were from Holland and then Australians and New Zealanders and some Canadians, we were all thrown in together. So, we were a pretty good size camp then and we were working on the airstrip. We had one guy get killed where the roller rolled over on him and killed him. But you worked every day. If you didn't work, you didn't eat. But anyway, when they moved us into this new camp, like I mentioned before, the best camp we went into, it was like four feet into the ground. There was now, our B-29s were really working on it and they were getting the best of it, so we were there. And this is something I want to bring up is that we were there when the Hell Ship showed up. And I am sure that I got, someplace I have a record of the Hell Ship when it showed up. And they took us down to help get these guys off. We were bad. Don't get me wrong. We were bad. These guys were badder. They were so weak that they didn't climb off that damn ship. They had locked them in the hold and they had crap all over them and urine all over them, and they just couldn't get out. So we helped carry them out of there. And it's probably one of the worst things I ever saw in my life. And the ridiculous thing that happened is in Cincinnati our milkman was a fellow named Vince Yakabushi. And Joe Yakabushi was on that ship. He died in my arms. He couldn't make it. No way in the world. He died. As a matter of fact, I talked to a fellow here who was a captain in the Philippines and he went through the Bataan death march, and they went through, it was terrible, too. But he died in my arms. And at that point Nash and I made up our mind, Nash was my best friend at the time, we're going to get out of this dam camp. What they had us doing there was digging caves to store some supplies and things because we were starting to be very effective with our bombing raids and that. And we were running, we were, it appeared that the American government, we were going to burn them out. So in Fukuoka, this is where we were now, the air raid must have started about like 9:00 o'clock at night and at 2:00 o'clock in the morning, the B-29s were still coming over and dropping incendiary and the place was all on fire. You could read a newspaper without a light. It was fire. That is when Nash and I decided we going to get out of here. And anyway, they were looking for volunteers to go to the coal mine. We volunteered to go. It couldn't be any worse, we figured. Hell, it couldn't be any worse than what we were at now. So Nash and I went to the coal mine up in Miata. And then they got a record of that, too. As a matter of fact, that is one the of the places we ended up there. This is a shaft mine. This wasn't a strip mine. So you go down in the shaft. The fleas and the lice were in the shafts. And this is where I weighed about fifty kilos then. That is right in between 100 and 110 pounds. And if you didn't work, you didn't eat. So, we were working in there and the food wasn't any better. And this is what I saved from that. Where is the other one? This is what they passed out. That was important. It told you that you were working and therefore you were entitled to some food.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Now that piece though was for anybody that worked on top of the mine. This one was if you worked in the mine. If you worked in the mine you got a piece of bread about that big (indicating) about that wide. If you worked outside the mine, you got a piece like that. So that is what they had and we lived on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So maybe if you worked in the mine, it was like six inches by two inches?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No not six inches.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not even six?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: More or less about maybe four, four and a half inches, three inches wide and about that thick.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That was it. And but on top of the mine, it was about maybe three inches square. Like that. That is what were you living off of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was this a day's ration?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, yeah, you had it for lunch. That was it. That is what you got for lunch. So, that is one of the few, those are a few other things. So, but the big advan -- Plus at the mine, after working in the coal mine was and we were in it -- As a matter of fact, I got a break there. They had -- I was in the mine initially and we weren't digging coal, we were rebuilding, the mine had collapsed so we were rebuilding the shaft. And we had a bunch of Englishmen with us and my friend Nash had got the job of staying outside running a little winch that when they pulled the cars up they'd hook the winch on and he would let the cars into the sorting yard and then the Korean people would go ahead and sort the coal. And the Englishman came to me and he said hey, why don't we just trade. You, I am down here in the coal -- I mean, I am on the outside and your friends and you're down here and all of my friends are down in the mine, I'd like to go with my friends. Hell, I'd love to get out of that mine. Because, see, normally when the safety light goes out in a mine, you leave the mine. But not in Japan. The guards would come over and relight the safety light. You just stayed there and keep working all the time. So I traded. And being outside on the mine, now we worked shifts. They had three shifts going all the time. So at night we used to ride around, we'd be able to get into the Japanese store and steal food and everything else. That was great for us. And then we went, but as far as working was concerned, the conditions were fleas, lice, filth, dirt, everything. But anyway, we had, we were on the day shift when we had just gone to work and the Japanese guard came running down hard. Matai, matai, matai. Kutch koi, kutch koi (ph). We had to come, we had to come, we had to come right away. Right away because they were calling us all to attention in the parade ground. The Japanese commander was there and he said he had good news for us. The war was over and we were going home. We were going home. It was good news. And of course, now, they sent these, our B-29s coming over now didn't bring bombs. Now they were carrying supplies in fifty-five gallon drums. And they had them tied to parachutes and they had break out of the para -- Hell, we didn't have a building in that there prison camp that had a complete roof anymore. They'd go right through the roofs. But we did, we had food and we had clothing. We had cigarettes then. I missed a lot probably not telling you, but anyway, the Japanese women were coming into our prison camp and they would do anything in the world. They would sew for you, they would cook for you, they would make you clothes, because we had stuff to gave them. And the Japanese women brought in a Japanese newspaper and on the front page was a picture of an American truck and an American tank and I said hey, doko des? Where is this? And they said well, that is Kagoshima. Osko (ph)? How do we get back down there? And they told us no way. This was, they had come and told us the war was over on about the 22nd Or 23rd of August and we were supposed to wait in that prison camp until MacArthur came and got us. Well, on the 7th of September, which is my birthday, is when we made up our minds we're not going to wait for MacArthur, we'll go meet him, you know. And it was kind of stupid because we never gave any thought to the Japanese people could have killed us or whatever and no one would have ever known the difference. So we busted out of camp. Walking down the road. In the meantime the English, our ranking officer in our camp was an English wing commander and he had taken English soldiers and put them in the watch towers and at the gate and wouldn't let anybody out and he had the Japanese rifles. They were going to shoot us if we -- we told them to go pound salt because we're going home. And you know, that is probably the first indication of any feeling that I had. We had worked with this old Japanese guy at the mine. He ran the big winch and we ran the little winch and he ran up to us and he was crying. And he told us that he was so glad we were going home. And he gave us a bottle of sake and a live chicken. So there is Nash and I and Harlan and Pruitt and Taylor, and I don't know who the other guy was, we were marching along and we got away and now we're going to go. And we also knew at that time where they sent our friend, I made a friend in Japan who became one of my best friends. He was a Black Dutchman. And his name was Eugene Pruhandaylala from Indonesia. I have got his name someplace here. And anyway, I knew the camp that they had sent him to. So on the way to Kagoshima, by the meantime when we got the word we were getting on a train, there was no railroad station left. Our bombers had completely flattened everything. The railroad cars were stacked on top of each other. We got on the train. As a matter of fact, we couldn't get on the train, really, we could kind of just hang on to it to start off with because the Japanese people were on the top of the train and the Kempaiahs saw this and they saw us so they came down and they ran all the Japanese out of this one railroad car. And we had a whole railroad car to ourselves, the six of us, they took pretty good care of us now. When we got to this town, I could find it I guess where I knew Eugene was, we got off, so we marched, we were marching through town with our live chicken and bottle of sake and a Japanese woman said hey, do we want her to fix the chicken for us? Well, sure. Took her about a half an hour to kill and dress and fix that chicken and we were eating it. And while we were eating, this has nothing do with it, but in the meantime, the treatment, as far as food and everything was, we had little things like that half full of rice, three times a day. At this point I weighed 50 kilos, now. I am 6'4" foot four. And then we ate there and some Japanese guy come in and said hey, was that our friend? Taylor had gotten into that sake and he was laying out in the gutter and we had to take Dick Taylor and take him with us. And we ended up in Gene's camp, Eugene, and what the Black Dutch had done in our camp, they had gone out and disarmed all the Japanese in the area. And they had, I could have got Samurai swords, and they had a two-story building in their camp where they just throwed them up and piled them up. Anyway, we, that night we got back on the train headed to Kagoshima. I fell asleep and I heard somebody say to me: "You son of a bitch, are you going to get off this train?" And I woke up and it was a guy from the 101st Airborne, MP, and he had all that new stuff. He didn't looks like we got -- when we did our fighting, it was with the 1903 Springfields and the old dishpan helmets and whatever it was. God, he looked good. Of course, I got off the train, got in a _____________ and they took us up. And they had brought a group in of 100 and first they had taken over a Japanese camp there and that is where we were and ran into a guy named Pough from Cincinnati and he gave me a carton of Hershey candy bars. I ate the whole carton that night. I ended up with diarrhea so bad the next day it was just terrible. Honest to God. But they got us together and they said they had a plane going to Okinawa and if we wanted to, he would take whoever he could to get on that plane. So well, I wasn't going to wait for any ship. I was getting out of Japan. I sat there squirming and about ready to crap in my pants. Got to Okinawa and Nash had left me the same night. We laughed about it. He left me on the airplane and I woke up and there I was by myself in the air -- got off, we were there for three days. Then they flew us to Manila. When we got to Manila, why, there is another story. I mean this was the place where they were prepared to invade Japan. So all the supplies and that were there. And you'd go through and as far as you could see were supplies. And they did everything they could. They took good care of us, of course, they were just -- and they were glad that, you know, they took really good care of us. And I know that -- I am getting close to the end of the story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, keep going, as much as you want to tell me.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Anyway, they were giving out like a check or something like that that entitled every soldier in the Philippines for three cans of beer that day. Lot of POW's were afraid to do it. I must have had a dozen of those tickets, so I ended up with three dozen cans of beer, you know. So me and the street sergeant, he would get a bunch of ice and we'd ice up the beer and play Pinochle all day. We were there for two weeks. And then they took us down to, put us on the troop ship to bring us home. And that was another -- it's funny, we got on this brand new troop ship. Hey, this isn't bad at all, air conditioned and everything else. Then they took us off the next day and marched us across and -- Here, what is left of it. This is the note I signed by the way. I told you they signed that they doled out for money when I first went over. They marched us across the dock and put us on the Joseph Dickman, World War I troop ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Alias the "Old Joe."

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Nash and I were four holds down. We slept out on the deck all the way home. And...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So this was a little newspaper booklet, whatever they printed on the ship?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. How long did that trip take?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I don't remember. I guess it was the best part of a week or so. I don't know. I know that I got aggravated with the Red Cross there because I went to see the Red Cross in Manila and I said I knew my brother was in the Marine Corps and was it possible that he was in the Philippines and they said that there were no Marines in the Philippines. So they knew that automatically. They told me that and they just ignored it. And when I got to, we got up to about where Honolulu was I got a cablegram from my brother. He was in the Philippines. He was twenty-five miles from where I was. And anyway, so, we went on into San Francisco and they had banners hanging on the bridge, welcome home, well done. One of the worse things of my life when we were getting off there was a, came over the speakers, they wanted to know if anything, if anybody knew about anything about Don Williams. His mother was waiting for him. I had a few things in my pockets that had been Don's. She cried. That was bad. It's a little about what happened to me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did Don die? Did he die in Wake?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, he died in that damn prison camp. He just, both Don and Cedric both kind of just gave up, you know. They got, I guess there was a pneumonia or whatever it was, they just died. We were burying one a day. And for what it's worth, at that time, I mean I guess it just didn't really sink in with me, you know, because I was the most important thing. And we ate roots over there and ate grasshoppers and we would string grasshoppers on a wire and throw them in the fire and eat them like peanuts. And the roots, they had one root over there about that big around (indicating). That was a, when you would find that, hell, that was good because everybody wanted that. That tasted like licorice. I ate a -- we had ate -- One time we ate that old toad. But anything to just stay alive is really what it boiled down to. And like I said, the Japanese, there was no medical care. When we ended up at the coal mining camp, that was another experience. I ended up with a bad tooth. Well, the only guy in the camp that had anything to do with the tooth was a Black Dutchman and he had a pair of forceps so you would go over to him and say, he would say what -- Arrr, arrr, over there, you know. So a couple of guys would hold you down and they would hold your mouth open and go POW! Mine came out okay. Just came out okay. Well, it wasn't good, but hell, we got it out. And Nash said to me how was it. And I said oh, it wasn't too bad. And so he went down. His came out in four pieces. He had a jaw that was like that (indicating). Well, of course he couldn't eat, so I helped, I took care of that for him. As a matter of fact, you were looking at that thing I made here, I can't translate it anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You can't make it out?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: For whatever it is, it's starting to...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I think pencil fades.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: It's fading and that...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It would be nice if you could get someone to type that up or something.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I started to try to do it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah, the lights -- What the hell is this here? But anyway, in here I kept a record of -- What we used to do is they'd give you maybe a bowl of rice or something today and we would, you would give us a bowl of rice let's say on a given day, like on your birthday or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: And there is a record of that in here, couple places, I know it's in here. Here is one of them. One rice. One rice. One was from Hemming and the other one was from Barney.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: So we'd have a big feast on our birthday or something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally go get back?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: You know, when I got home, I sent the telegram to my mother. I told her I was coming home, coming home at 5:00 o'clock in the morning. Well, when I got to the railroad station, there wasn't anybody. If I got home at 5:00 o'clock at night, and I was a little disappointed and I got in that taxi cab with my stuff. By the time I got home, I jumped out of the cab and ran in that side door and up that flight of stairs and I know I buried my head my in my mother's lap. You know, for what it's worth, they would never take me prisoner again. Never. You go through the abuse and everything else that you went through just to stay alive. That is all we did. And, you know, you saw the picture they had the audacity of building a monument to us. That is kind of ridiculous. When I got home, I got a friend out in South Dakota yet. Bridge was with me. As a matter of fact this is the only man that I knew that was at Nagasaki when they dropped the atomic bomb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: And well, Bridge is Bridge. He always reminded me a little bit of -- He was older than I was, he was five years older than I was, so I used to lean on him a little bit when we were in the prison camp. I don't know if you are aware of this or not but these are some statistics from...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You got home probably, what, late 1945?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I got home in, yeah, I got out of the prison camp on my birthday and I got home, it was probably September, sometime in October. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is a --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: These are actual figures.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: World War II, 130,000 captured interned. 14,000 died while POW.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: See them buried from one to the other.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: The casualty thing in Japan was 37 percent. The Germans was one percent.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Germany was, pardon, what?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: One percent.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: We were, the Japanese were 37.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Which is where my dad was unusual, because in fact, I think two thirds of the two hundred guys in his labor camp died --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Did they?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- from malnutrition and that was way out of line with what happened.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That surprises me. But this is Bridge here. And here is the four guys. That's Nash and I and Bridge and Smythe this is an old picture.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were in the camps in Japan, were you able to get any war news about how the war was progressing?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Oh, that was funny. That was funny. Yeah, we got it. The Japanese told us how they were winning the war. When we were on Wake Island, now we had a Zenith Trans Ocean thing up in the ____________ so every night somebody would slip up to there and get the news from the United States. We'd hear what, find out what was going on. Now, it's like you, it's kind of hard to believe everything you read in the newspaper. Because one time the -- See, we were getting bombed by the Americans now on Wake Island, because the Japanese had stopped and the Americans were bombing us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: And one time when they were letting us shoot our missile there on Wake and we had all kind of ganged up down around there, we looked up and looked up and sure as hell, there was a flight of B-17s come over, three of them. And they were right over the top of the island. The Japanese didn't even know it. And of course, they spotted them about the time we did. They took off and they ran over and got to their anti-aircraft and got in their Zeros and went out after them. And that afternoon, about 3:00 or 4:00 o'clock they called us out on the parade ground and they said they caught up with them. Shot them all down. That is it. Well, we went up and got the news from the States and they said, United States reported a raid on Wake Island. They destroyed everything on the ground and everything else. Hell, they didn't even hit the ground. The Japanese didn't shoot them down. You kind of wonder who was the biggest liar. Oh, God. Yeah, I look back and I have feelings and well, you saw that right here, you know, I can -- They would never take me prisoner again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any chance at all to, for any distractions when you were in the Japanese prison camps? I couldn't say entertainment, but any kind of --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, we kind of created your own as far as that was concerned. One time after the Black Dutch and them telling us why we, they had us put on like a show and these Indonesians were just unbelievable when it came to talent. Hell, they made musical instruments out of cigar boxes and things and they were just absolutely great. Yeah, we did that. Then we had a guy, I don't know, he was a Westerner, and I never realized there were Westerners but he was from down here in the West Indies and he was English and he would dance with a glass on top of his head. But most of the time you were so hungry, the biggest, the whole topic, if you would look through there or that, a lot of things about food in that. It was just all you were interested in was trying to find something to eat or something, whatever it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid images that come to mind when you think about that?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, I guess not. Maybe sometimes things will pop up, but I think about all different things, plenty of things. I know Bridge, one time, while we were still on the island, see, we were helping them unload the ships and that but when there wasn't a ship to unload, why we -- This was from my hat, my old campaign hat. I don't know what ever happened to that. Cigarettes from where they dropped them and Red Cross packages and that. But, we were over on Peale Island and apparently, on Peale is where the warehouse for the canteen was and Bridge had found a gallon can of what was chocolate syrup and it was punctured and that. So we brought that out and we got to eating it. And then Bridge got the idea, well, he is going to make some hot chocolate. So he went ahead and I don't know how we really even had a fire there, and we had been eating it now And the flies came to the top of the hot chocolate. The flies had got to the chocolate syrup before we did. Oh, God. This Doctor Shank we had was just a tremendous person. And he was from Indianola, Indiana and I told you he saved my life. But he taught us things like how to make cottage cheese. See, the Japanese, we had a bunch of what they called Klim on the island, which was powered milk. They didn't want that. They gave that to us. And we couldn't drink it all, so we had no refrigeration, the Klim would go sour. So Doctor Shank says well, all we have to do now is to get a plumbers torch and bring that thing to a boil and it will convert it into cottage cheese for you. Well, we did that. He had us build a thing that keeps stuff cool. He was a brilliant guy. He showed us things. Oh, another thing, Bridge always brings is up. He said the time that we were out unloading the ship, we saw the comfort women. They brought them to Japan, the ones that they wrote about in that. Anyway, we broke loose one night and these barges were big, you know, and we were floating around on the ocean with this in this sea-going, this barge, for two days we were out there. And we didn't know what the hell was going to happen. But that is Bridge's his helmet. He said man, they said send out the -- The Japanese had like, I guess it was a little patrol boat. They would come out and they finally brought us back to Wake Island. Hell, we didn't know where we would have ended up if we had stayed on that thing. And no, I am sure there are things that I would remember if I called them up. But I know that the conditions were bad. There was no food. That is all anything, you could get something to eat was the most important thing. Staying alive was the most important thing really, just staying alive. I feel great that I could have been part of what we did out there on Wake, you know, we did, what we accomplished there as far as they were concerned.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I want to make sure I am clear on one thing. The fellow from the Hell Ship, the mailman, was that in fact the mailman from Cincinnati?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, no, that was his brother.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was his brother?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Joe Yakabushi, Joe, and his brother was Vince Yakabushi.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know him before the war?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, I didn't. We met up. I helped carry him off the ship. He couldn't get off. Took him back to where our camp was and they were putting him up there and Joe was sleeping between Nash and I, we were trying to warm him up and he died. He couldn't make it. It's an interesting thing that a lot of people talk about going to see that show, The Bridge on the River Quai. There is a dead POW for every railroad tie on that God damned thing. That is how bad it was. And it's just -- It's incredible what they did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Pretty much so. Let me show you a few things here that I showed you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is an amazing collection of stuff and I hope you preserve it.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Like when I go to Kenston, when you leave I'll call Kenston and tell them I'll meet at seven, we have seven classes out there that I'm going to.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That is great.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I don't know, I think this is going to be my last year of speaking. I get tired. I am getting tired.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you get a good reception from the students?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Just tremendous. There is some of the stuff you see there. Room 109, Mr. Arnold Green. There is stuff that they have given to me. Thank you, Mr. Arnold Green. I stuck it on the door that day. Kids are good. Kids are good. And our history books are so, they don't have anything in it. There is about a page and a half that deals with World War II. And I'm not the only one. I mean, I have got, Jack Lloyd is out there and these guys are out there and you're going to be talking to Saul today.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I am talking to Saul Weiss two days yet on Thursday. I talked to Jack Lloyd.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Did you talk to Jack?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Couple months ago.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Jack is a fine guy, quite a guy, too. Everyone -- It was all bad. Don't get me wrong. And I have got to believe that anybody that was a prisoner has a story and they are going to bury.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I have talked to a lot of barbed wire buckeyes in the last few months.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A lot. And I have got my dad's story on tape. Fortunately, he recorded it before he died.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I did too and I gave a tape to each one of my children.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I don't want them to ever forget what they did to me. (Interruption of audio) While we're there, the papers had always picked it up and they said that the commander, the officer, when they -- oh, that is another thing that really gets to us. Our relief, our relief was one day away and they turned them back and sent them back to Pearl Harbor. One day away. I understand that the Marines and that, they were just almost ready to rebel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why did they send them back?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: I think the admiral then who was in charge of Pearl Harbor was afraid that they would lose the aircraft carrier that was there. And but then, they said well, if they had sent them, what we were doing, the Japanese lost 11 ships there, that is where the 5000, 7000 casualties were. They lost 11 ships. They lost 42 airplanes. Knocked their damn, knocked their brains out. There was a --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I see little marks here. These are guys that you knew, personally?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, those are little check marks. Those are guys that I knew. Lot of times I get a lot of things from, someone might say to you my father was there on Wake or something like that and I am able to go ahead and have a picture made and blow it up and send it to them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That is pretty amazing.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: There are not many of us left.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many do you think are left that were on Wake Island?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, the last time we got together it was maybe 40, maybe 50.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And what did you say -- I am sure it's on the tape here but, originally how many were on Wake Island?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, there was roughly 1150 contractors, civilians. And there was 350 -- 379 First Marines, 50 Airmen, 70 Pan Am, 1146.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let me do a quick math on this. 1700 maybe 17, 1800 total and you say you inflicted what, 5- or 6000 casualties?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Between 5- and 7000 Japanese.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 7000 Japanese?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: We lost 124.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Lost 124. Sank two destroyers.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: No, sank 11 of their ships.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 11 ships overall, right?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: 11 total, including a light cruiser and a transport. Shot down 42 planes including, and we also sank a submarine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. That is a story that doesn't get told a whole lot. Well, it's amazing that you had the foresight to bring a lot of that stuff back from the prison camps?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Well, I didn't bring that much really. Those little things like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Those little things, exactly.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: You know, I could have got, and you know they say about well, the guns and that. Hell, I wasn't interested in that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Kind of souvenir --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: That was the last thing I was interested in. I gotta keep this record here. This is a ________. That is a picture of the dam.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is this dam still there?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Dam is still there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that near a big city in Japan?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yeah, it's near Fukuoka, near Sasebo. Sasebo is where they train the navy office. Did. This is where, if you ever get to Honolulu, a friend of mine went over there and took this. This is the spot where all the guys are buried in Punch Bowl.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I have been to the Punch Bowl.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Right at Punch Bowl, that is where we are. Right. You remember when you went to Punch Bowl, you went to the bottom?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: And you walk up to where the Memorial --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: If you are at the bottom, if you walked 100 feet that way --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I probably saw it.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: -- there is a plaque on the ground.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think I did.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: And that is -- That is our guys.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About fifteen years ago I went there.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: This is the coal mine camp that I was in. We can't get any satisfaction -- We really don't want any. As far as money settlement officially --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So it was a Mitsubishi mine, huh?

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: Yep, oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You weren't near Richard Francese, were you? He was also --

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: He was in northern, he was in Honshu, he was in a copper mine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Copper mine, yeah, that is right. Talked to him about two years ago I think it was.

sp.speaker: Arnold R. Green
sp.p: This is more what, this is Admiral Cunningham. He was our Commander Cunningham on Wake Island, but he ended up as Commander of the display, they have it down in Pensacola. This is his complete story about what took place on Wake Island. I walked in there and said hey, I understand that Commander Cunningham was here and they said oh, it's all over there. They have got a whole wall about what he did. No, I don't, you know, people, they say forget. I'll never forget. Murray Kidd, Canone, Pat Hockey, Fred Kelley, I knew them all. Orville _______, maybe some I knew better than others, but, knew them all. And buried a lot of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. [End of Interview]
